content.content:
=== GOTCHAS ===
- THE BIG ONE — never use `ingestion_strategy: FULL` against a das__staged view that can hold more than one row per primary key. Each execute silently inserts one extra duplicate row into <entity>_desc (22 -> 23 -> 24 -> 25 across three runs in my test), forever, and NONE of the presentation views show it: view_CUSTOMER stayed at 3 rows and view_CUSTOMER_hist at 4 rows the whole time. Since the DAS design is dlt landing parquet, an append/merge write disposition makes das__staged append-style by construction. Use FULL_LOG as the default; reserve FULL for views you can prove are exactly one row per key (dlt `replace` disposition). Switching back to FULL_LOG stops the bleeding but does NOT clean up rows already leaked — you must truncate <entity>_desc and re-execute.
- ANY other open connection to the .duckdb file makes `daana-cli execute` fail, INCLUDING a read-only one, and the error message is a lie: 'daana framework is not installed on the remote database. Run daana-cli install first...'. The real DuckDB lock error is swallowed and does not appear even at --log-level debug. In this architecture the marimo app reading dar__uss, a dlt pipeline, or a stray `duckdb` REPL will all trigger it. The build needs an explicit single-writer discipline (a lock file, or a supervisor that stops readers before running the DAB step), and whoever operates it must be told that this error means 'the file is busy', not 'run install'.
- Object names on DuckDB PRESERVE the model.yaml entity-id casing: view_CUSTOMER, CUSTOMER_focal, ORDER_CUSTOMER_x — not the lowercase view_customer PostgreSQL produced. Any DAR/USS generator that hardcodes lowercase names from the PG run will still work (DuckDB resolves case-insensitively, verified all four of view_customer / VIEW_CUSTOMER / "view_CUSTOMER" / "view_customer"), but code that string-matches names out of information_schema WILL break. Either lowercase model.yaml entity ids, or normalize when reading the catalog.
- <entity>_focal and <entity>_idfr are created but stay EMPTY on DuckDB (0 rows for both CUSTOMER and ORDER) even though execute reports the 'execute_idfr_pipelines' phase as succeeding. All data is in <entity>_desc + <src>_<tgt>_x. If the DAR/USS generator was designed against the PostgreSQL run and joins to _focal or _idfr, it will produce empty results on DuckDB. Build DAR on the view_* layer only.
- The presentation views are `SELECT * FROM dab.f_CUSTOMER()` — DuckDB TABLE MACROS. Macros do NOT appear in information_schema.tables or information_schema.routines-style catalog queries you might write by habit; you need duckdb_functions(). Any 'is DAB deployed?' health check that only looks at information_schema.tables will see the views but miss the macros they depend on.
- view_<entity>_with_rel carries NO relationship key columns — its column list is byte-identical to view_<entity>. The name suggests it denormalizes the foreign keys; it does not. Get relationship keys from view_<src>_<rel>_<tgt> (ORDER_key, CUSTOMER_key, type_key, eff_tmstp, ver_tmstp).
- Every numeric attribute comes back as DECIMAL(28,8) regardless of source type (my DECIMAL(12,2) became 220.25000000). marimo/plotting code downstream should format explicitly rather than trusting the source scale.
- `daana-cli version` is not a command (Error: unknown command "version"). The version flag is `-v` / `--version`. Trivial, but it will waste a minute in CI.
- The daana-cli --help text lists 'Multi-database support (PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, Oracle, SQL Server)' — DuckDB is NOT advertised. It works fully, but this is unadvertised/possibly-untested territory, which is consistent with the FULL duplication bug and the empty _focal/_idfr tables. Do not expect DuckDB parity to be maintained by the vendor.
- deploy is re-runnable after editing a mapping (I changed ingestion_strategy and re-deployed four times, always exit 0). execute is re-runnable and idempotent under FULL_LOG and under TRANSACTIONAL, and only non-idempotent under FULL-on-multi-row-source.

=== OPEN QUESTIONS ===
- Whether <entity>_focal and <entity>_idfr are populated on the PostgreSQL run. I only observed DuckDB (both empty). If PG populates them, this is a DuckDB-specific defect worth reporting to the vendor and worth guarding in the DAR generator; if PG is also empty, they are simply vestigial and DAR should ignore them.
- What FULL vs FULL_LOG do on a DELETE — i.e. a key that disappears from the das__staged view on a later load. I ran out of time-box before testing this. This is the remaining strategy difference the build depends on: does FULL tombstone/close the row (row_st flips from 'Y'), or does the entity stay in view_<entity> forever? The _desc table has row_st, sta_tmstp and end_tmstp columns that are all currently 'Y'/NULL/NULL, so the machinery for it exists — but I did not exercise it.
- Whether the FULL duplication is triggered specifically by multiple rows per primary key, or by the mid-stream switch from FULL_LOG to FULL. I inferred the former because the duplicate appeared only on attributes sourced from the multi-row customers view (type_key 11) and never on the single-row loyalty view (type_key 8, also FULL), and because it recurred +1 per run long after the strategy switch. I did not run a clean FULL-from-scratch-on-a-multi-row-view test to prove it.
- Whether daana-cli can be pointed at a DuckDB file via an ATTACHed database or a read_only connection, which would sidestep the single-writer problem. I only tested the plain `database: ./warehouse.duckdb` form.
- Whether the relative path in `database: ./warehouse.duckdb` is resolved against the CWD or against the connections.yaml location. I always ran from the project directory, so the two coincided.
- The exact daana-cli / focal-cli version. `daana-cli version` is not a valid command and I did not spend a call on `-v`.
- Whether concurrent daana-cli invocations (two entities in parallel) would deadlock. The 'bounded parallelism' in the help text is intra-process; I did not test two daana-cli processes at once, but given that even a read-only holder breaks it, they will almost certainly conflict.

=== VERSIONS ===
- duckdb (Python package) == 1.5.5
- CPython 3.11.15 (selected by uv)
- uv-created venv at ./.venv
- daana-cli at /home/user/adss-fable-poc/bin/linux-amd64/daana-cli — version NOT captured (`daana-cli version` is not a valid command; I did not run `-v`)
- focal-cli — invoked internally by daana-cli (seen in debug log as `command=focal-cli`), version not captured

4

21	- Model once, generate the rest
22	
23	Every analytics team pays the same tax, and almost none of them have it on a line item.
24	
25	It works like this. The business asks a question. Someone builds a star schema to answer it: pick the fact, pick the grain, pick the dimensions, wire up the keys, test the measures. The next question arrives, and it doesn't quite fit the first star, so someone builds another. Then a third. Before long you have a galaxy of star schemas, each one a small hand-built artifact, each one slightly out of step with its neighbors, all of them drifting apart as the business changes underneath them.
26	
27	We have learned to call this normal. It is not. It is the cost of building the consumption layer by hand, one question at a time.
28	
29	And the parts that hurt are the parts nobody warns you about. The fan trap, where one join quietly doubles your revenue. The "which fact table do I even query" conversation that every new analyst has to relearn. The moment a measure means one thing in the sales mart and something subtly different in the finance mart, and a meeting gets spent reconciling two numbers that were never modeled the same way.
30	
31	## The wrong argument
32	
33	So the usual debate is which star schema to build. Snowflake it or keep it flat. One fact table or several. Conformed dimensions or not.
34	
35	That is the wrong argument. The question is not which star schema to build by hand. The question is why we are building them by hand at all.
36	
37	Because we already model the business. If you run a proper business layer (DAB, in the Daana stack: the layer where you model entities, keys, relationships, and history the way the business actually sees them) then everything a consumption model needs is already declared. The grain, the relationships, the measures, they're all sitting right there. Building a star schema by hand is typing out something the model already knows.
38	
39	So let the model generate it. An earlier piece on this blog, The Design of Analytical Data Storage Systems, made the case that star schemas belong in the consumption layer (DAR, Data According to Requirements: the layer shaped to what the consumer needs), not in the business layer. This is the other half of that argument: what the consumption layer should actually be, and where it should come from.
40	
41	## What a Unified Star Schema is
42	
43	The pattern that makes this work is the Unified Star Schema, and credit where it is due: it is Francesco Puppini's, from his book of the same name with Bill Inmon. I'm not going to reinvent it here, just show what happens when you generate it on top of a business layer.
44	
45	The idea is a single table, the bridge, that connects every entity to every other entity it can legitimately reach. When I talked it through with Puppini, he suggested calling it a "super fact" rather than a bridge, to break free of what "bridge" means in the Kimball world. The name fits. It holds all the relations and all the measures in one place.
46	
47	 topology // `the puppini bridge`
48	
49	 
50	 
51	
52	the Puppini bridge: one hub every entity connects toIn a USS you stop sorting tables into facts and dimensions. Every entity can play both roles. An order is a thing you measure and a thing you slice by. So is a customer. So is a product. You connect each one to the bridge, and the end user joins whatever they care about to that single structure. No fan traps, because the bridge is built to never fan out. No "which fact table", because there is one.
53	
54	There is one more move that earns the "answers almost everything" claim, and it is about time. Instead of one row per entity instance, you make the bridge event-based: one row per measurement event, each carrying its own date. An order placed sets the date to the order date. An order shipped sets it to the shipped date. An order due sets it to the required date. Now every measure, across every process, lands on one canonical calendar. You can ask "what happened in Q1" across orders, shipments, and returns on a single timeline, without stitching three star schemas together. One calendar, every process.
55	
56	## Cascading inheritance
57	
58	If you do not care how the bridge gets built, skip to the next section. All you need is that the generator works out the safe paths for you. For everyone else, the mechanism is simpler than it sounds.
59	
60	You walk the business model as a graph. For each entity, you follow the relationships that go from many to one and inherit the keys and measures of everything you reach. An order line points to one order, the order points to one customer, so the order line inherits both. The rule is short: follow any path that never fans out, and inherit everything along it.

138	## Why one model answers the vast majority
139	
140	This is where the decision-maker payoff lives.
141	
142	Because the model knows which measures are additive along which dimensions, the USS can answer the vast majority of analytical questions without anyone choosing a fact table or second-guessing a grain. And it's self-describing. The same model that builds the bridge also knows, for every measure and every dimension, whether you can slice that measure by that dimension, and how. That's a sliceability contract, and it doesn't have to live in a proprietary corner. Express it as a vendor-neutral semantic contract (e.g. OSI) and any BI tool or AI agent can read it directly. 198	the sliceability contract: every question is a lookupTwo things follow from that. First, coverage is not a matter of faith. Because the list is explicit, you can read off exactly which questions the model answers and which it does not, before you trust it with anything. Second, this does not replace your BI tool, it feeds it. You point Power BI, Tableau, or Qlik at the bridge, or build your semantic model on top of it, instead of hand-building a star for every report. And do not skip the most used analytics tool on the planet just because it is unfashionable to mention it: Excel. It's not going anywhere, and ignoring it is futile. A single bridge is a PivotTable's best friend. Point Excel at the bridge and an analyst can slice the whole model, on one calendar, without waiting on anyone to build them a thing.
199	
200	That is the real difference between a hand-built star and a generated USS. A hand-built star answers the questions you anticipated when you built it. A generated USS answers the questions the business model makes valid, which is a far larger set, and it tells you which ones those are.
201	
202	## Why generated, not hand-built
203	
204	The economic argument almost writes itself.
205	
206	A hand-built consumption layer scales with the number of questions. More questions, more stars, more maintenance, more drift. A generated one scales with the number of changes to the business model, which is a much slower clock. You model a new entity once, regenerate, and every analysis that can now reach it gets it for free. Consistency stops being a discipline you have to enforce and becomes a property of how the thing is built.
207	
208	This is the same shift my colleagues have written about in The Rise of the Model-Driven Data Engineer and Contract-Driven Data Transformation: stop writing the artifact, declare the model and generate the artifact. In practice I generate the USS from a handful of small YAML files, and it takes seconds.
209	
210	## One model, any shape
211	
212	Here is the part that usually ends the debate.
213	
214	Once you've modeled the business, you haven't committed to one consumption format. A USS is one shape you can generate. So is a data mart, One Big Table, a classic star, a feature table. They're all projections of the same model.

238	one model, any shape: every consumption format is a projectionWant a data mart for the finance team? It's not a separate build. It's a selection: take the entities finance cares about, generate the shape they need. Want One Big Table, because your tool or your data scientist prefers a single flat table? You can generate it flat, from the model or from the USS. Want a classic star, or a feature table? Same story.
239	
240	You are no longer choosing between a USS, a star, an OBT, and a mart, and arguing about which is right. You model the business once, and you generate whichever shape the consumer in front of you needs. The shape is a detail. The model is the asset.
241	
242	## The honest trade-offs
243	
244	None of this is free, and I would rather say where it costs than pretend it does not.
245	
246	Many-to-many relationships have no fan-out-safe direction, so the generator skips them and warns you. If your domain leans hard on many-to-many, you will model around it, and that is real work. There are genuinely non-additive measures, ratios and distinct counts across the wrong grain, where you still have to think. The USS does not abolish thinking. It removes the busywork so you can spend the thinking where it actually matters.
247	
248	The bigger cost is upstream, and I would rather name it than hide it. All of this rests on a business layer that is actually modeled well. The USS doesn't model your business for you. It generates the consumption layer from a business model you still have to get right, which means the hard work doesn't disappear, it moves to where it belongs: defining your entities, your keys, and your relationships once, properly. Get that layer right and everything downstream generates. Get it wrong and the generated USS will faithfully reproduce the mess.
249	
250	And then there is the objection I hear most: a single bridge across everything must be slow to query. So I benchmarked it instead of arguing about it. I put the same questions to a Unified Star Schema and to an equivalent multi-fact star schema, on TPC-DS at scale factor 100, and the query performance held up. There was no meaningful penalty for unifying. The scare story about USS falling apart under load is, in my experience, just a story. It builds fine too: a bridge of roughly a billion rows reloads in about four minutes on an F64, and you can load it incrementally, by key or by updated-at, rather than reloading at all.
251	
252	## Model once, generate the rest
253	
254	We have spent years getting very good at hand-building consumption models. We got so good at it that we stopped noticing the bill.
255	
256	But the business layer already knows the grain, the relationships, the measures, and the history. The consumption layer is downstream of all of it. So model the business once, carefully, and let the consumption layer generate itself. The star schema, the Unified Star Schema, the OBT, the mart, the feature table: not things you build, things you select.

content.content:
---
name: dar
description: Work on the DAR layer — the generated Unified Star Schema, dab/uss.yaml, and the SQL under dar/uss. Use when adding an event or a measure, changing the bridge's column contract, debugging a total that is wrong or multiplied, or when generated SQL and the model have drifted.
---

# DAR — data according to the requirements

One bridge, one peripheral per entity, one calendar. **Nothing here is hand-written**, and a
wrong name is fixed in the model and regenerated. An edit to generated output is lost on the
next generation, and until then the code and the model quietly disagree.

## The shape

```
dab/uss.yaml        the declarations: events, their dates, their measures
dar/uss/*.sql       generated and committed
```

`uv run adss dar generate` writes them; `--check` fails if the committed SQL is not what the
model produces; `uv run adss dar build` runs them.

## The column contract

Everything downstream is written against these names and will not survive them changing. A
model change **appends**; it never rearranges.

| column | what it is |
|---|---|
| `_stage` | the entity this row is a row *of* |
| `_event` | the event, lower-cased |
| `_event_date` | joins `_calendar.date_key` |
| `_is_current` | always true on a transaction stage |
| `_observed_at` | the DAB effective timestamp, which is the DAS extraction time |
| `<entity>_key` | one per entity, in model order |
| `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` | one per measure; **non-null only on the owning stage** |

## The one rule that matters most

**Keys inherit; measures do not.** A stage carries the key of every entity it reaches along
many-to-one relationships, and a measure is non-null only on the stage that owns it. Copying a
parent's measure onto its children multiplies it when summed — that is the fan trap, and
avoiding it is the entire reason there is a bridge rather than one wide join.

Two consequences at query time, neither of which the schema can enforce:

- A join on the row's own `_stage` key may be `INNER`. A join on an **inherited** key must be
  `LEFT`.
- A ratio is `sum(a) / sum(b)` at query time. It is never a stored measure: an average of
  averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at.

## Adding a measure

Add it to `dab/uss.yaml` under its event, with a **definition** — the glossary copies these
verbatim and never composes one. Name it `<descriptor>_<entities>_<unit>`, entity plural, no
scope or aggregation words: `placed_orders_count`, never `total_orders`. Then regenerate.

## Things worth knowing

- The generator reads `view_<entity>_hist` and keeps the latest version **in which the event's
  date is set**, so an entity the event never happened to has no row for it by construction
  rather than by a filter someone has to remember.
- It never reads `_focal` or `_idfr` (empty on this platform) or `_with_rel` (no relationship
  keys, despite the name).
- **It never invents a member.** A null dimension stays null. A question that wants nulls
  grouped or excluded says so in its own file, because that is a property of the question.
- Layout is the linter's, applied *inside* the generator. Do not hand-format emitted SQL and
  do not run a formatter over `dar/uss` afterwards — either produces a diff on every
  regeneration.
- A zero-edge walk is a valid walk. One entity and no relationships is the normal case.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# MODEL TEMPLATE  –  edit & rename before use
#
# WHAT IS A MODEL?
#  A model defines your business entities (like CUSTOMER, ORDER, PRODUCT)
#  and how they relate to each other. It's the foundation of your data
#  transformation pipeline.
#
# STRUCTURE:
#  • model metadata    – ID, name, definition
#  • entities          – business objects (CUSTOMER, ORDER, etc.)
#  • attributes        – properties of entities
#  • relationships     – how entities connect
#
# TYPICAL WORKFLOW:
#  1. Define your model in this YAML file
#  2. Compile it: daana-cli compile model -i model.yaml -o model.json
#  3. Generate mapping templates: daana-cli generate template mapping --model model.json --all-entities --dir mappings/
#  4. Deploy to database: daana-cli deploy
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

model:
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # 1) Model metadata
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  id: MY_BUSINESS_MODEL           # REQUIRED – unique identifier (letters, digits, underscores)
  name: MyBusinessModel            # REQUIRED – human-readable name
  definition: Core business entities and relationships  # one-liner
  description: |                     # free-text, Markdown allowed
    This model defines the core business entities for my organization,
    including customers, orders, and products, along with their
    relationships and key attributes.

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # 2) Entities – your business objects
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  entities:
    # Example entity: CUSTOMER
    - id: CUSTOMER_ENTITY
      name: CUSTOMER
      definition: A person or organization that purchases products or services
      description: Represents customers in our system with their contact and demographic information

      attributes:
        # Simple attribute example
        - id: CUSTOMER_NAME_ATTR
          name: CUSTOMER_NAME
          definition: Full name of the customer
          description: The customer's full legal name
          type: STRING              # Options: STRING, NUMBER, START_TIMESTAMP, END_TIMESTAMP, UNIT
          effective_timestamp: true    # Track historical changes (true/false)

        # Group attribute example (for related values)
        - id: CUSTOMER_ADDRESS
          effective_timestamp: false
          group:
            - id: CUSTOMER_ADDRESS_LINE1
              type: STRING
            - id: CUSTOMER_ADDRESS_CITY
              type: STRING

    # Example entity: ORDER
    - id: ORDER_ENTITY
      name: ORDER
      definition: A purchase transaction
      description: Represents customer orders with amounts and timestamps

      attributes:
        - id: ORDER_TOTAL_ATTR
          name: ORDER_TOTAL
          definition: Total order amount
          type: NUMBER
          effective_timestamp: true

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # 3) Relationships – how entities connect
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  relationships:
    - name: PLACES                    # Relationship name
      definition: Customer places order  # What it means
      description: Indicates which customer placed which order
      source_entity_id: CUSTOMER_ENTITY # Entity that 'owns' the relationship
      target_entity_id: ORDER_ENTITY    # Entity being related to

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# TIPS:
# • Start with 2-3 core entities, you can always add more later
# • Each entity gets 5 identifier slots automatically (_IDFR_01 through _IDFR_05)
# • Use groups for related attributes (e.g., address components, time periods)
# • Set effective_timestamp: true for attributes that change over time
# • Compile before materializing: daana-cli compile model -i model.yaml -o model.json
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

content.content:
daana-cli is a command-line interface for the Daana platform that transforms raw operational
data into business-ready analytics 100x faster than manual ETL pipelines.

Key Features:
  • YAML-based data modeling (entities, attributes, relationships)
  • Automatic template generation for models, mappings, and workflows
  • Built-in validation and linting for all configurations
  • One-command deployment to database
  • Bounded parallelism for data transformation workflows
  • Multi-database support (PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, Oracle, SQL Server)

Quick Start Workflow:
  1. init       - Create project with template files
  2. install    - Set up framework in your database
  3. (edit model.yaml and connections.yaml to define your data)
  4. generate   - Create mapping templates for entities
  5. (edit mappings to connect to your data sources)
  6. check      - Validate your configurations
  7. deploy     - Deploy workflow to database
  8. execute    - Run data transformations

Learn more at https://github.com/daana-code/daana-cli

Usage:
  daana-cli [command]

Available Commands:
  check       Validate configurations (model, mapping, workflow, connections)
  completion  Generate the autocompletion script for the specified shell
  deploy      Deploy workflow to database
  doctor      Diagnose environment health and configuration issues (not implemented yet)
  execute     Execute a workflow with data transformations
  generate    Generate template files for different components
  help        Help about any command
  init        Initialize a new Daana project with template files
  install     Install the Daana framework into a database
  lint        Lint a data model YAML file
  merge       Synchronize mappings with updated model definitions
  ui          Launch the local Daana UI in a browser

Flags:
      --config string              Config file (default: ./config.yaml or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/daana/config.yaml)
      --dump-events string         Write focal-cli's raw progress event stream (NDJSON) to this file; for regenerating TUI fixtures
  -h, --help                       help for daana-cli
      --log-level string           Set the log level for both console and file (trace, debug, info, warn, error, fatal, panic)
      --log-level-console string   Set the console log level (trace, debug, info, warn, error, fatal, panic)
      --log-level-file string      Set the file log level (trace, debug, info, warn, error, fatal, panic)
      --no-tui                     Disable TUI elements (logo, progress bar) for clean log output
  -v, --version                    version for daana-cli

content.content:
---
id: q01
slice: 1
status: green
persona: Sales director
question: How many orders were placed per order month and destination country?
aggregation: count
measure: ORDER.PLACED_ORDERS_COUNT
dimensions: [_calendar.month_label, order.destination_country]
time_grain: month
defines:
  - ORDER
  - ORDER.PLACED_ON
  - ORDER.DESTINATION_COUNTRY
  - ORDER.events.PLACED
  - ORDER.measures.PLACED_ORDERS_COUNT
order_by: [order_month, destination_country]
---

## Story

As the **sales director**, I want to see how many orders were placed per order month and
destination country, so that I can put sales effort where demand is moving.

## Definitions

Every term below is defined in `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` and nowhere else. This
question references them; it does not restate them.

- {{ORDER}}
- {{ORDER.PLACED_ON}}
- {{ORDER.DESTINATION_COUNTRY}}
- {{ORDER.events.PLACED}}
- {{ORDER.measures.PLACED_ORDERS_COUNT}}

## The W's

- **Why**: demand moves between countries and between seasons, and sales effort should
  follow it rather than lag it by a year.
- **What**: the count of orders placed. Not their value, not their contents, not whether
  they were ever delivered.
- **Who**: customers place them; the sales director is the one who acts on the answer.
- **How**: one `placed` event per order, counted at the month of the day it was placed.
- **Where**: the country the order is to be delivered to, which is not necessarily where
  the customer is.
- **When**: all history, at calendar month (`_calendar.month_label`, `YYYY-MM`).
- **What will you do with it**: move sales effort toward the countries whose monthly counts
  are rising, and ask why for the ones that are falling.

## Nulls

Both dimensions are nullable in the source metadata, and neither is null in the recording.

Both queries nonetheless take the same position, for the same stated reason rather than by
coincidence: an order with no date on which it was placed has no `placed` event, by
construction in the generated layer, and the control query mirrors that with
`WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL`. A null destination country would be kept as its own group
by both — the generator never invents a member, and the control does not either.

## Delivered

![The answer as it was accepted](answer.png)

The presentation this question was accepted on, as it stood at that commit. The blueprint
asks that what was delivered and when is recorded; the picture beside the question is that
record, and it is why a later reader can tell whether the answer they are looking at now is
the one somebody acted on.

## Answers

Two queries, in `staged.sql` and `uss.sql`. The first computes the answer straight from what
the source sent, bypassing the business model and the star schema entirely. The second
computes it from the star schema. They must agree row for row.

That check does not prove the answer is *right* -- a wrong definition would make both wrong
together. It proves that routing the number through integration and generation did not
change it, which is the failure this architecture is most exposed to and least able to see.
=== uss.sql ===
-- The answer, from the generated star schema. This is what the destination reads.
SELECT

# A business question is the unit of delivery, carried as a data file with the two queries that must agree on its answer

## Context and Problem Statement

At the coffee machine, "how were sales last quarter?" works, because both people share years of
context. A dashboard has none of it. The gap between that question and one a data system can
answer is the actual work: an answerable question names its aggregation, its measure, its
dimensions and its time grain, and defines every term that two people might read differently.

This system delivers in slices, and a slice is accepted on a presentation of one question's
answer. So the question is not documentation *about* the work — it is the specification, the
acceptance test, and the thing the page renders. That makes its format load-bearing in three
directions at once, and it has to satisfy constraints that pull against each other.

`dab/model.yaml` is the only place the data is explained (B8), so a question may not restate a
definition — but it must carry enough that a reader can answer it without a conversation. The
acceptance test compares two business queries, but no test may contain business vocabulary
(conventions §6). And the check that gives the slice its confidence — computing the answer twice
and requiring agreement — is only worth anything if the two computations are genuinely
independent, which is a property nobody can enforce mechanically.

## Decision Drivers

* a question is answerable from the file alone, with no conversation
* definitions are referenced, never restated, and every reference is proved to resolve
* the acceptance test names nothing from the business
* the two queries are independent enough that agreement means something
* the question survives being reprioritised, refined or pivoted, which the methodology expects

## Considered Options

* A question directory holding `question.md` plus the two queries as `.sql` files
* A single markdown file with the SQL in fenced blocks
* Questions as test functions in `tests/`
* A recorded expected result committed alongside, with no second query

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: **a directory per question under `docs/questions/NN-<slug>/`, holding
`question.md` and the two queries as `staged.sql` and `uss.sql`.**

Separate `.sql` files rather than fenced blocks, for a reason that is not aesthetic: `.sql` files
are linted by the same sqlfluff hook as every other statement in the repository, and
[conventions §3](../conventions.md) already refuses to let SQL hide inside a string. A fenced
block is a string. The moment the acceptance queries are exempt from the SQL rules, they become
the least-reviewed SQL in a repository whose whole claim rests on them.

*The file is a data file, and that is what keeps the test clean.* The runner discovers question
directories, reads the front matter, runs both queries and asserts agreement — naming nothing. A
per-question test *function* would smuggle the vocabulary back in through its own name, so the
runner is parameterised over what it finds.

*Definitions are referenced by identifier.* The front matter lists the model identifiers the
question depends on, and the prose cites them by token rather than by paraphrase. A machinery test
asserts every token resolves to something `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` defines. When a
question needs a term the model does not define, the question is **blocked** and the model change
comes first — which is not an obstacle but the methodology working: a question the model cannot
answer has found a gap in the model, and finding it is what asking was for.

### What the two queries actually prove, and what they do not

This deserves to be stated honestly, because it is easy to oversell.

The control query computes the answer from `das__staged.<table>__current`, bypassing DAB and DAR
entirely. The other computes it from `dar__uss`. CI asserts they agree row for row.

What it catches is the failure this architecture is most exposed to and least able to see: that
routing a number through integration and generation *changed it*. Dropped rows from a join, a
multiplied measure, a mis-inherited key, a version collapse that kept the wrong row, an event
filter that excluded more than it meant to — all of these show up as a number that no longer
matches the source.

What it does not catch is a wrong definition. If the model says an order is placed on its shipped
date, both queries can be written to that and both will be wrong together. Nor does it catch a
failure the staged layer shares — and there is one specific case worth naming: the engine's
duplicate-row defect is invisible in every presentation view, so both queries would agree while
the history quietly corrupted. That is why a separate data check counts the base table directly.

The risk that the two are written to agree rather than to be right is real and cannot be designed
away. Three things reduce it. The queries read different schemas in different vocabularies, so a
transcription is visible as one. The control query is forbidden from mentioning `dab` or
`dar__uss`, so it cannot consult the answer it is checking. And when they disagree,
`dab/model.yaml` is the named arbiter: the query that departs from the definition is the one that
changes, never both until they match. Without that last rule the cheapest repair is to make the
check agree with itself, which deletes the only thing it was measuring.

A recorded expected result was the alternative. It is simpler and it catches every regression
exactly — but its first recording is only as right as the query that produced it, and after that
it can only confirm the system still agrees with its own past. It is a regression test, not a
reconciliation, and this layer needs the second.

### Lifecycle

`status` is one of `draft`, `red`, `green`, `superseded`. The methodology expects a question to be
validated, refined or pivoted once the business sees real data, and all three are wins — so a
refinement edits the question in place and a pivot supersedes it with a new one, keeping the
original with its status set. What the business asked for before it saw the answer is part of the
record of why the model looks the way it does.

One question, one slice, one branch, one page. The page reads the question's own `uss.sql`, so the
presentation and the test cannot disagree about what was asked.

### Consequences

* Good, because the specification, the acceptance test and the rendered page are one artefact,
  which is what makes the prototype the deliverable rather than a report about it
* Good, because the acceptance queries are linted like all other SQL
* Good, because a question that outruns the model is blocked visibly rather than answered
  approximately
* Bad, because every answer is written twice, which is duplicated effort and a second thing to
  maintain when a definition changes
* Bad, because the control query has a shelf life. It stays writable only while a question needs
  no integration; from the first question spanning two sources, writing it against the staged
  layer means reimplementing DAB inside the check. Slice 6 is where that bill arrives, and this
  record does not pay it
* Bad, because "independent" is a property of how the queries were written and nothing enforces
  it. The arbiter rule limits the damage; it does not prevent the sin

### Confirmation

`tests/test_questions.py` asserts every question file parses and every definition token resolves
to the model. `check_question` enforces both halves of the boundary rule — the control query
mentions neither `dab` nor `dar__uss` and *does* read a `__current` view, and the answer query
reads `dar__uss` and reaches past it for nothing — because the page runs the answer query verbatim
and a reach past DAR would render, pass, and be exactly the dependency the flow rules exist to
prevent.

The declared dimensions are asserted against the **answer** query only. An earlier draft of this
record claimed both; that was wrong, and the check caught it on its first run. The control query
says the same thing in the source's own words, and requiring the same spelling in both would force
one to be written from the other — which is precisely the independence this whole arrangement is
for.

`adss check` runs both queries against the built warehouse and asserts row-for-row equality. Both
suites name nothing from the business.

---
name: dab
description: Work on the DAB layer — dab/model.yaml, the mappings, and the modelling engine. Use when adding an entity, attribute or relationship, editing anything under dab/, running install/deploy/execute, or debugging engine errors, history that looks wrong, or rows that multiply.
---

# DAB — data according to the business

The layer that breaks the dependency between source and consumption. It is also **the only
place the data is explained**: every definition lives here and everything else references it.

## The shape

```
dab/model.yaml           entities, attributes, relationships -- and their definitions
dab/uss.yaml             what the generated layer needs: events, measures (see the dar skill)
dab/mappings/*.yaml      one per entity: how it is loaded from das__staged
dab/workflow.yaml        the model plus its mappings
dab/connections.yaml     one profile
bin/linux-amd64/daana-cli  the engine, vendored, pinned by the checksum beside it
```

## Adding an entity

1. Add it to `dab/model.yaml` in **business language**. No source word may appear — not in an
   id, a name, a definition or a description. If you are typing the source's word for
   something, stop and ask what the business calls it.
2. Add `dab/mappings/<entity>-mapping.yaml`, then add it to `workflow.yaml`.
3. `uv run adss dab deploy && uv run adss dab execute`.

Every entity, attribute and relationship needs a `definition` written for a person. A missing
one is a blank row in a glossary somebody notices in a screenshot.

## The seven mapping rules

They are in `docs/conventions.md` §1.4 and checked by `tests/test_mapping_rules.py`, because
**the engine checks none of them**. Two are not style:

- **M3 — `FULL_LOG`, always.** `FULL` against a source with more than one row per key inserts
  a duplicate row on every run, forever, and *every presentation view hides it*. Our staged
  change log is multi-row-per-key by construction, so `FULL` is exactly the wrong default and
  its failure is invisible in both of a question's acceptance queries.
- **M2 — exactly one primary key.** Two entries are read as two *alternate identifiers*, not
  as a composite key, and that mode cannot be undone once loaded. Compose with
  `concat(cast(a AS VARCHAR), '-', cast(b AS VARCHAR))` — the separator is not cosmetic.

## What the engine does and does not do

The whole type vocabulary is `STRING`, `NUMBER`, `UNIT`, `START_TIMESTAMP`, `END_TIMESTAMP`.
There is no plain date type; a business date is `START_TIMESTAMP`.

A version is dated by `entity_effective_timestamp_expression`, which is always `extracted_at`
here — so DAB's history is what the system observed and when. That wins even when the entity
has a `START_TIMESTAMP` attribute; confirmed, not assumed.

## Things that cost a day if you do not know them

- **`daana framework is not installed on the remote database` means the file is busy.** The
  lock is per process: the engine is a subprocess, and it cannot take the lock while we hold
  it. `require_detached` refuses before that happens; if you see the message anyway, close
  whatever has the warehouse open.

# The SQL style. docs/conventions.md section 3 records why each setting is what it is.
# The duckdb dialect is required, not preferred: postgres cannot parse QUALIFY.
[sqlfluff]
dialect = duckdb
templater = raw
max_line_length = 120
# AL09 forbids `x AS x`, which is exactly the every-column-aliased discipline that makes a
# UNION branch positionally safe. RF06 fires on every mixed-case identifier crossing over from
# DAB. LT05 and LT09 are line-layout opinions a generator should not have to implement.
# ST06 wants simple columns before calculations. A generated view's column order mirrors
# its contract's declaration order, so the two can be read side by side; reordering to
# please a linter would delete that property.
exclude_rules = AL09, RF06, LT05, LT09, ST06

[sqlfluff:indentation]
indented_joins = false
indented_using_on = true

[sqlfluff:rules:capitalisation.keywords]
capitalisation_policy = upper

[sqlfluff:rules:capitalisation.functions]
extended_capitalisation_policy = lower

[sqlfluff:rules:capitalisation.identifiers]
extended_capitalisation_policy = consistent

[sqlfluff:rules:capitalisation.types]
extended_capitalisation_policy = upper

[sqlfluff:rules:convention.casting_style]
preferred_type_casting_style = cast
=== sqlformat.py ===
"""Generated SQL is laid out by the same formatter that lints it.

The conventions say a tool's configuration is the rule wherever a tool can check one. This
extends that: the linter's own formatter decides layout, so the generator cannot drift from
it, and a rule change is picked up by regenerating rather than by hand-editing an emitter.

It runs inside the generator rather than after it, so the committed file is already the
formatted one and a regeneration produces no spurious diff.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

import sqlfluff


class SqlFormatError(Exception):
    """The generator emitted SQL the linter could not parse."""


def formatted(sql: str, config: Path) -> str:
    """Lay out generated SQL, refusing to write anything the linter cannot parse."""
    try:
        fixed = sqlfluff.fix(sql, config_path=str(config))
    except Exception as broken:  # sqlfluff raises several unrelated types
        raise SqlFormatError(f"the generator emitted SQL the linter rejected: {broken}") from broken
    if not fixed.strip():
        raise SqlFormatError("the formatter returned nothing, which means it failed to parse")
    return fixed if fixed.endswith("\n") else fixed + "\n"

=== model.yaml ===
# The only place the data is explained. Everything else -- contracts, questions, the
# generated layer, the pages -- references these definitions and never restates one.
#
# No source name appears here. Not in an id, not in a name, not in a definition. This is the
# layer whose whole purpose is to be independent of where the data came from, so a source's
# word in it would mean the dependency had been moved rather than broken.
model:
  id: ADSS
  name: ADSS
  definition: What the business means by the things it records.
  description: >-
    One model for the whole platform. Entities arrive as the questions that need them arrive,
    and a new attribute, entity or relationship is always a new structure rather than a change
    to one something already depends on.

  entities:
    - id: ORDER
      name: ORDER
      definition: >-
        A commitment by the business to supply goods, created when it accepts a customer's
        request for them.
      description: >-
        One order is one such commitment. It begins on the day the business accepts it and is
        settled by delivering what was promised, to where it was promised.
      attributes:
        - id: ORDER_NUMBER
          name: ORDER_NUMBER
          definition: The number the business uses when it refers to one particular order.
          description: Unique across all orders, and never reused once issued.
          type: STRING
          effective_timestamp: false

        - id: PLACED_ON
          name: PLACED_ON
          definition: The day the business accepted the order, and from which the order exists.
          description: >-
            An order is placed once. This is the date every question about when demand
            occurred is measured against.
          type: START_TIMESTAMP

        - id: DESTINATION_COUNTRY
          name: DESTINATION_COUNTRY
          definition: The country the business has undertaken to deliver the order to.
          description: >-
            Where the goods are going, which is not necessarily where the customer is. A
            question about demand by geography means this unless it says otherwise.
          type: STRING
          effective_timestamp: true

        - id: FREIGHT_CHARGE
          name: FREIGHT_CHARGE
          definition: What the business paid to have this order carried to its destination.
          description: >-
            One amount for the whole order, not per item, and it is a cost of fulfilling the
            order rather than anything the customer was billed for. Nothing states the
            currency -- there is only one, and no record of which -- so it is whatever
            currency the business keeps its books in. That is a gap to be filled, not a
            convention to be relied on: two currencies added together would look exactly
            like this.
          type: NUMBER
          effective_timestamp: true

    - id: CUSTOMER
      name: CUSTOMER
      definition: >-
        A party the business has agreed to supply, and against whom orders and payment are
        recorded.
      description: >-
        One customer is one such party. It exists from the moment the business is willing to
        accept an order from it, independently of whether it has ever placed one.
      attributes:
        - id: CUSTOMER_CODE
          name: CUSTOMER_CODE
          definition: The code the business uses when it refers to one particular customer.
          description: Unique across all customers, and never reused once issued.
          type: STRING
          effective_timestamp: false

        - id: TRADING_NAME
          name: TRADING_NAME
          definition: The name the customer trades under, and is addressed by.
          description: >-
            What a person would call the customer. Not a legal or registered name, which the
            business does not record.
          type: STRING
          effective_timestamp: true

        - id: BASED_IN_COUNTRY
          name: BASED_IN_COUNTRY
          definition: The country the customer itself is in.
          description: >-
            Where the customer is, which is a different question from where an order is going
            -- see DESTINATION_COUNTRY. A question about who is buying means this; a question
            about where goods move means that. They coincide often enough that using one for
            the other is easy and wrong.
          type: STRING
          effective_timestamp: true

  # No cardinality is declared, because the modelling language has nowhere to declare it: a
  # `cardinality` field is rejected outright, and `type` accepts any string and is dropped on
  # compile. Writing `type: "1:N"` here would read as a statement the engine never receives.
  # That an order has one customer is inferred from the mapping's shape and pinned by a data
  # check instead. ADR 0006.
  relationships:
    - name: IS_PLACED_BY
      definition: The customer whose request the business accepted when it created this order.
      description: >-
        An order is placed by exactly one customer, and by the same one for its whole life:
        this records who asked for the goods, not who is billed or who receives them.
      source_entity_id: ORDER
      target_entity_id: CUSTOMER
=== uss.yaml ===
# What the generated star schema needs to know that the business model does not otherwise
# say: which date makes an entity a measurement event, and which numbers are its measures.
#
# These are business facts -- "an order is placed on a day, and counting orders means
# counting orders" -- so every one carries its own definition. The glossary copies these
# strings; it never composes one. Names follow docs/conventions.md section 2.
uss:
  events:
    - id: PLACED
      entity: ORDER
      definition: >-
        An order was placed: the business accepted a customer's request and committed to
        supplying it. One per order, on the day it was accepted.
      kind: transaction
      date_attribute: PLACED_ON
      measures:
        - id: PLACED_ORDERS_COUNT
          definition: >-
            The number of orders placed. One for each order, counted on the day the business
            accepted it, regardless of what was on it or whether it was ever delivered.
          aggregate: count

        - id: FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT
          definition: >-
            What the business paid to have placed orders carried, attributed to the day it
            accepted each one. It is a cost of fulfilment, so it is additive over any set of
            orders and over any period -- but only over orders, since one order carries one
            freight charge however many items are on it.
          aggregate: sum
          attribute: FREIGHT_CHARGE

# How one entity is loaded from what the system recorded. This is the one artefact whose job
# is to bind two vocabularies, so it names both -- but only in table, primary_keys and
# transformation_expression. See docs/conventions.md section 1.4.
entity_id: CUSTOMER
mapping_groups:
  - name: default_mapping_group
    tables:
      - connection: dev
        table: das__staged.customers
        primary_keys: [customer_id]
        ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG
        entity_effective_timestamp_expression: extracted_at
        attributes:
          - {id: CUSTOMER_CODE, transformation_expression: customer_id}
          - {id: TRADING_NAME, transformation_expression: company_name}
          - {id: BASED_IN_COUNTRY, transformation_expression: country}
=== build/check cli ===
def check() -> None:
    """Assert what the built warehouse contains. Requires a build."""
    project = Project.discover()
    with reading(project.warehouse) as connection:
        findings = run_checks(project, connection)
    for finding in findings:
        typer.echo(f"{'PASS' if finding.passed else 'FAIL'}  {finding.check}")
        if not finding.passed:
            typer.echo(f"      {finding.detail}")
    if any(not finding.passed for finding in findings):
        raise typer.Exit(1)


@app.command("build")
def build(
    live: Annotated[bool, typer.Option(help="Read the source instead of the recording.")] = False,
) -> None:
    """Build the whole system, in the one direction data flows.

    Each step is a separate command because the layers fail differently and are debugged
    separately. This is them in order, which is the order a reader should meet them in.
    """
    das_ingest(live=live)
    das_unpack(check_only=False)
    dab_install()
    dab_deploy()
    dab_execute()
    dar_generate(check=False)
    dar_build()
    typer.echo("built")


@app.command("shoot")
def shoot_destination() -> None:
    """Photograph the destination, for the pull request the slice is accepted in."""
    project = Project.discover()
    image = shoot(project.destination, project.screenshots, project.browser_cache)
    typer.echo(f"{image} ({image.stat().st_size:,} bytes)")

commit 55edbd7f2268cdc05f204d7ce2f02f927b99b329
Author: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
Date:   Mon Sep 7 22:41:42 2026 +0000

    docs(adr): decide where an inherited key comes from, and correct what slice one assumed
    
    The first relationship is the first thing that inherits, so the generator has to get a parent
    key onto a child row. The engine offers four objects to take it from, they disagree with each
    other, and their names do not say which is which. A probe built a two-entity model, moved a
    foreign key, and read every object the engine produced.
    
    It overturned two things ADR 0002 states as fact, and both were wrong in the direction of
    comfort. The relationship view is a current view, not a historical one: it partitions by the
    child, so a changed foreign key does not lose its row -- it re-points every one of that
    child's rows at the new parent and erases the old pair, retroactively and invisibly. And
    view_<E>_with_rel does carry relationship keys, on the target side, along with every attribute

7	
8	# An inherited key is resolved from the raw pairs, as of the observation time of the row that inherits it
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	Slice 1 built a bridge with one entity and no relationships. ADR 0002 asserted that one shared
13	bridge is safe because keys inherit along many-to-one edges while measures do not, and said in as
14	many words that the walk had zero edges and the property was asserted rather than exercised. This
15	slice is the first with an edge: an order is placed by a customer, and the question groups the
16	freight of an order by the *customer's* country, which exists nowhere on the order.
17	
18	So the generator has to get `customer_key` onto an order row. The engine offers four places to get
19	it from, they do not agree with each other, and the names do not say which is which. A probe built
20	a two-entity model with one relationship, changed a foreign key, and read every object the engine
21	produced. It overturned two things ADR 0002 states as fact.
22	
23	**The relationship view is a *current* view, not a historical one.** ADR 0002 says reading it would
24	lose a row whose foreign key changed. That is not what happens. The macro behind
25	`dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is:
26	
27	```sql
28	rank() OVER (PARTITION BY <SRC>_key, type_key ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC) AS nbr
29	... WHERE nbr = 1 AND row_st = 'Y'
30	```
31	
32	Partitioned by the child, so the child never drops out — it is re-pointed. After the probe moved
33	CH1 from P1 to P2, the pair table held both rows with `row_st = 'Y'` and the view held `CH1|P2`
34	alone. Nothing is lost; the *old* pair is what is lost, for every row of that child, retroactively.
35	The reason to read the raw pairs is therefore history, not disappearance, and ADR 0002 got the
36	right answer from the wrong mechanism.
37	
38	**`view_<entity>_with_rel` does carry relationship keys — on the target side, and it fans out.**
39	ADR 0002 says its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`. That is true only for the
40	relationship's *source* entity. Once an entity is a relationship *target*, its `_with_rel` view
41	becomes a double left join through the pair macro and gains the source entity's key **and every one
42	of its attributes**, one row per child. The probe measured the consequence:
43	`sum(CHILD_AMOUNT)` over `view_PARENT_with_rel` returned 200.75 against a true 150.75. That is a
44	live fan trap in a view whose name invites exactly the join that springs it.
45	
46	**`rank()` is not `row_number()`, so a tie returns both rows.** The probe's CH5 had two parent codes
47	in one load, so two pair rows shared an `eff_tmstp`, and the relationship view returned CH5 twice.
48	A child appearing twice in the bridge multiplies its measures — the precise failure the bridge
49	exists to prevent, arriving from the engine's own view rather than from anything we wrote.
50	
51	**The model cannot say that an edge is many-to-one.** This is the finding that decides how the rule
52	is enforced, and it is settled by the engine's own error rather than inferred: adding
53	`cardinality:` to a relationship is rejected with *"Valid fields are: name, definition, description,
54	source, target, source_entity_id, target_entity_id, type"*, and that list is the whole grammar. The
55	one candidate, `type`, is not a cardinality slot — it accepts any string without validation
56	(`1:N`, `MANY_TO_ONE`, `BOGUS_VALUE` all pass `check model`) and is **dropped on compile**: it does
57	not appear in the compiled `model.json` and never reaches the engine. Nor is the engine merely
58	silent about cardinality. It is agnostic by design: it treats a child's parents as a *set*,
59	aggregating all target keys per `(source key, eff_tmstp)` into a fingerprint and writing a row when
60	that set changes. Many-to-many is a supported case, not a defect.
61	
62	So the generator cannot learn "many-to-one" from the model, and it cannot learn it from the data,
63	because the data is legitimately allowed to be many-to-many. Something else has to say it.
64	
65	## Decision Drivers
66	
67	* a measure summed over the bridge is additive at every grain, whatever the model's shape
68	* a bridge row is true as of one instant, and every column on it is true as of that same instant
69	* the generator reads objects whose behaviour has been observed, never ones whose names suggest it
70	* a case the design cannot handle fails the build loudly rather than answering a question wrongly
71	* the walk works for zero edges, one edge and, later, a chain — without a special case per depth
72	
73	## Considered Options
74	
75	* `dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the engine's ranked relationship view
76	* `dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the raw pairs plus a relationship name, ranked here
77	* `dab.<SRC>_<TGT>_x` — the pair table directly, with `dab__meta` for the type key
78	* `dab.view_<TGT>_with_rel` — the view named as though it were for this
79	
80	## Decision Outcome
81	
82	Chosen option: **`dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, ranked in the generated SQL as of the child row's own
83	`_observed_at`, one parent per child, with the tie refused by a data check.**
84	
85	`v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is the raw pair table joined to the engine's metadata to add a `rel_name`
86	column, with no ranking and no `row_st` filter. That is what makes it the right source: the pairs
87	arrive unfiltered, and the as-of rule is ours and visible in the generated SQL rather than the
88	vendor's and hidden in a macro. It also solves a naming problem the pair table has on its own — the
89	pair table is named `<SRC>_<TGT>_x` from the *entity pair*, not from the relationship, so two
90	relationships between the same two entities land in one table separated only by a `type_key` whose
91	meaning lives in `dab__meta.atom_contx_desc`. Filtering on `rel_name` says what is meant; filtering
92	on `type_key = 1` says nothing and breaks when a second edge is declared.
93	
94	**As of `_observed_at`, not as of now.** The stage picks a version of the child; the inherited key
95	is the one in force when that version was observed. Today the stage always picks the child's latest
96	version, so this coincides with the current parent and the choice looks free. It is not: it is what
97	keeps the rule stated at the level of a bridge row rather than at the level of a table, so it
98	survives a stage that keeps more than the latest version, which is what a snapshot event and a
99	`_is_current = FALSE` row will both need.
100	
101	**Exactly one parent per child, and a tie is a build failure.** Since neither the model nor the data
102	can state the cardinality, it is inferred from the mapping and then pinned. The inference is sound:
103	M5 already forbids an attribute expression from containing a subquery, an aggregate or a reach into
104	another table, so a relationship's `target_transformation_expression` reads its own row and is
105	single-valued per staged row *by construction*. What that does not cover is one key appearing on
106	several staged rows of a single load, which is exactly how the probe's CH5 acquired two parents at
107	one instant. So the check is not optional decoration on top of the inference — it is the half of the
108	argument the inference cannot make.
109	
110	The generated SQL uses `row_number()` over `eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC` and then the parent key
111	itself, so it is deterministic and can never emit two rows for one child. `ver_tmstp` is not a
112	formality: the engine writes a closing row that shares its predecessor's `eff_tmstp` and is
113	separated from it only by `ver_tmstp`. Determinism alone would be a silent wrong answer, so a
114	generated check counts children with more than one open parent at the ranking instant and fails the
115	build when it is not zero. The two together mean the bad case is loud, and that if the check is ever
116	ignored the damage is a mis-attributed row rather than a doubled measure. Doubling is worse: it is
117	invisible in both of a question's acceptance queries if both are written the same way.
118	
119	**Only open pairs.** The read filters `row_st = 'Y'`. The engine flips a pair to `'N'` in exactly one
120	case — the source row disappears from `das__staged`, and `FULL_LOG`'s delete branch closes it — and
121	it keeps both rows when it does. In this architecture `das__staged` is an append-only view over
122	parquet, so that should never fire; the filter is there because "should never fire" is not a reason
123	to read a retracted pair if it ever does.
124	
125	`view_<TGT>_with_rel` is refused outright and now for a measured reason rather than an assumed one.
126	The engine's ranked view is refused because its as-of rule is not ours to state and its `rank()`
127	can fan out. The pair table is refused because it cannot name the relationship it is carrying.
128	
129	**A child with no parent keeps its row and inherits a null key.** The probe's CH6 has no pair row at
130	all, so the join is a left join. An order the source attributes to nobody is still an order that
131	was placed, and dropping it would change a count that ADR 0002 already published. Null is not a
132	member: it groups as itself and the generator invents nothing for it, per conventions §1.3.
133	
134	### Corrections to ADR 0002
135	
136	ADR 0002 is not superseded — its decision stands and this record extends it. Two of its factual
137	claims are wrong and are corrected here rather than in place, because what a record was when it was
138	made is the thing that makes it worth keeping:
139	
140	1. "A changed foreign key keeps its row, which reading the relationship view would not have done."
141	   The relationship view does keep the row. It re-points every one of that child's rows at the new
142	   parent and erases the old pair, which is a different defect and a worse one, because it is
143	   invisible.
144	2. "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship key columns at all; its column list is
145	   byte-identical to `view_<entity>`." True on the source side only. On the target side it carries
146	   the source entity's key and attributes, fanned out.
147	
148	The check ADR 0002 installed for the second claim asserted it of *every* entity, so it fails the
149	moment CUSTOMER becomes a relationship target. That is the check working: it was pinning observed
150	behaviour and the behaviour was mis-observed. It is replaced by one that asserts the real rule —
151	the source side is unchanged, the target side gains exactly the source entity's columns — which is
152	a stronger statement than the one it replaces and would have caught this in slice 1 had it been
153	possible to write then.
154	
155	## Consequences
156	
157	* Good, because the as-of rule is written in the generated SQL, so a reader of `dar/uss/_bridge.sql`
158	  can see when the inherited key was true without reading a vendor macro
159	* Good, because the fan-out the engine's own views expose cannot reach the bridge: the generator
160	  emits `row_number()`, and the case that would have needed it fails the build first
161	* Good, because filtering on `rel_name` makes a second edge between the same two entities a new
162	  structure rather than a silent collision
163	* Good, because the walk is the same shape at zero edges and one, so slice 5's two-hop chain extends
164	  it rather than special-cases it
165	* Bad, because the generated bridge SQL grows a ranked CTE per edge, and at three or four edges it
166	  stops being readable in one screen. It is generated, linted and drift-checked, so this costs
167	  legibility rather than correctness
168	* Bad, because `v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is an engine-internal object with no compatibility promise,
169	  like every other object here. The pinning checks are what turn a vendor change into a failure
170	  instead of an empty column
171	* Bad, and not fixable here: **a foreign key set to null is never retracted.** The engine's reader
172	  filters the pair source on the target key being non-null, so "this child now belongs to nobody" is
173	  inexpressible — re-landing a child with a null parent writes no row, no tombstone and no `row_st`
174	  flip, and the stale pair survives forever. The probe reproduced this. If the source ever nulls an
175	  order's customer, DAB keeps the old customer and nothing says so. That is a property of the
176	  engine, not of this decision; it is recorded here because this is the decision that would
177	  otherwise be blamed for it
178	
179	## More Information
180	
181	The probe found one thing that is not used and should be, when there is a reason to. Every
182	presentation object wraps a DuckDB table macro taking a `p_eff_tmstp` with a default, so the whole
183	DAB layer is point-in-time queryable for nothing: `f_child_parent_x(TIMESTAMP '2026-01-15')` returned
184	the January parent while `f_child_parent_x()` returned the current one. That is a second, shorter
185	way to write the as-of join. It is not taken because it moves the as-of rule back inside a vendor
186	macro, which is the thing this decision is spending SQL to avoid — but a later slice that needs
187	as-of over several objects at once should weigh it again rather than rediscover it.
188	
189	`type_key` is not stable across models: it was 1 for the relationship in this probe and 17 in an
190	earlier one, and attribute type keys differ per entity within a single model. It is never
191	hardcoded — `rel_name` is what the generated SQL matches on, which is the whole reason
192	`v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is read rather than the pair table it wraps.
193	
194	## Confirmation
195	
196	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts the generated bridge left-joins the pairs rather than inner-joining
197	them, that it ranks by `row_number` and not `rank`, that the ranking is as of the child's
198	`_observed_at`, and that a non-owning branch still emits a typed null for a key it does not own —
199	this last one because a union takes its column names from its first branch, so the order of the key
200	columns is the invariant and counting them would not catch a transposition.
201	
202	A generated data check counts children with more than one parent at the ranking instant and must
203	return zero. Another counts bridge rows whose inherited key resolves to no row in the target
204	peripheral, which is the shape a mis-spelled M6 target expression takes: the engine reports nothing
205	at deploy or at execute, and the column is simply null everywhere.
206	
207	The engine-behaviour checks are widened rather than removed: `_focal` and `_idfr` are still empty,
208	`view_<E>_with_rel` is unchanged on a relationship's source side and gains exactly the source
209	entity's columns on its target side.
210	
211	What this slice still does not prove is the fan-out property itself. Both entities here are at the
212	same grain — one order has one customer — so no measure can multiply across the edge no matter how
213	the join is written. The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the
214	test that a parent's measure is not multiplied by its children becomes possible. Saying so is the
215	point: ADR 0002 asserted this property in slice 1 and it is still asserted now.
216
